issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner-wife is entitled to the transfer of the divorce petition.

facts: The petitioner-wife filed a petition to transfer a divorce case initiated by her husband.

While this transfer petition was pending, the respondent-husband filed an application asking the Supreme Court to use its special powers under Article 142(1) of the Constitution to grant a divorce immediately.
The husband argued for the divorce based on the irretrievable breakdown of the marriage, highlighting the multiple litigations, criminal complaints filed by the wife, and his subsequent arrest.
law: The wife's transfer petition was filed under Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
The husband's application for a final divorce decree was filed under Article 142(1) of the Constitution, which allows the Supreme Court to pass any order necessary to do complete justice.
application: The Supreme Court decided to first address the husband's application for a final divorce decree before considering the wife's request to transfer the case.
The Court noted that the fate of the transfer petition depended on the outcome of the husband's application for divorce.
By exercising its extraordinary powers under Article 142(1) to dissolve the marriage, the Court rendered the original divorce proceeding (which the wife sought to transfer) moot.
Since the marriage itself was dissolved by the Supreme Court, there was no longer a pending divorce case to be transferred.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the wife's transfer petition because it resolved the underlying marital dispute directly by granting a decree of divorce under Article 142(1). This action made the transfer of the original divorce case unnecessary, and the petition was consequently disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether this Court, upon the application filed by the respondent-husband, can exercise its powers u/Art. 142(1) of the Constitution to grant a decree of divorce to the parties on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.

facts: The respondent-husband filed an application before the Supreme Court under Article 142(1) of the Constitution.
The application sought a decree of divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
This application was filed during the pendency of a transfer petition initiated by the petitioner-wife.
The wife opposed the granting of divorce, arguing that her consent was necessary.
Previous divorce petitions filed by the parties under the Hindu Marriage Act (HMA) had been unsuccessful.
law: The Supreme Court's power under Article 142(1) is distinct from that of a Family Court, which is bound by the fault-based provisions of divorce laws like the HMA.
Under Article 142(1), the Court can depart from standard procedures and substantive laws to do "complete justice" between the parties.
The consent of both parties is not required for the Court to grant a divorce under Article 142(1). This power is specifically invoked to do substantial justice when one party does not consent.

When considering such an application, the Court's role is not to assign fault but to take a holistic view to determine if the marriage has irretrievably broken down and if there is no scope for reconciliation.
application: The Court rejected the wife's submission that her lack of consent prevented the dissolution of the marriage, stating that the power under Article 142(1) is meant for situations where mutual consent is absent.
Instead of delving into the allegations and counter-allegations to find fault, the Court acted as a "problem solver" and took a holistic view of the relationship.
The Court assessed the circumstances and concluded that there was an irretrievable breakdown of the marriage between the parties.

Based on this assessment, the Court found it to be a "fit case" to exercise its extraordinary discretion under Article 142(1) to dissolve the marriage, while also noting the need to protect the wife's financial interests.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the husband's application and exercised its powers under Article 142(1) of the Constitution to grant a decree of divorce, dissolving the marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown, despite the wife's opposition.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Article 142(1) of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has the jurisdiction to pass any decree or order necessary to do complete justice in a pending matter, which includes the power to dissolve a marriage on the grounds of irretrievable breakdown, even if one of the spouses opposes the dissolution.
obiter: A serious relook of the entire provision is warranted by the legislation. It is also a matter of common knowledge that exaggerated versions of the incident are reflected in a large number of complaints. The tendency of over implication is also reflected in a very large number of cases.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's power under Article 142 of the Constitution to dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown is specifically meant to be invoked in cases where one of the parties does not consent to the divorce. If both parties consented, they could use the standard procedure for a decree of divorce by mutual consent. The very purpose of this extraordinary power is to do substantial justice between the parties when a marriage is factually over but one spouse opposes the dissolution.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a dissolution of marriage is necessary to do complete justice between the parties, in which case the court can exercise its power under Article 142(1) of the Constitution of India, even if one of the spouses opposes the prayer.
When granting a divorce under Article 142, the court must ensure the financial interests of the wife are protected so that she does not suffer financially in the future or have to depend on others.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner-wife's submission that a marriage cannot be dissolved under Article 142 without the consent of both parties has no substance.

The court reasoned that the powers under Article 142 are required to be invoked precisely in a case where one of the parties does not agree and give consent, in order to do substantial justice between them.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that it has the power under Article 142(1) to grant a decree of divorce where necessary to do complete justice, even if one of the spouses opposes it.

The court's reasoning established that the absence of the wife's consent was the exact scenario for which the invocation of Article 142 powers is intended, as mutual consent cases can be handled by competent courts through standard procedures.
policy_considerations: The ultimate object of justice is to find out the truth and punish the guilty and protect the innocent.

When exercising its extraordinary power to dissolve a marriage, the court must protect the interest of the wife financially so that she may not have to suffer financially in the future and may not have to depend upon others.
